lower-0862-s9-test-a-claim.description: Use totals, ordered outcomes and scale factors to justify conclusions across topics.

sections.title: Whose visits count in the mean?
sections.label: Combine counts
sections.intro: A group mean tells you the total per person if everyone shared it equally. Multiply by the headcount to recover the total. The same idea works backwards when the combined mean is known and one group mean is missing.

blocks.html: A combined mean is the sum of the group totals divided by the combined headcount. A larger group has more weight.

figure.alt: One group of four people and another group of nine.
figure.caption: A person in either group counts once. Use the group sizes to combine group means.

blocks.prompt:
The table gives the numbers of library visits made by the members of two clubs.

ClubMembersMean visits
North87
South1313

Find the mean number of visits per person for both clubs combined. Give an exact answer.
blocks.hint: Recover the totals using the two headcounts, 8 and 13. The denominator of the final mean counts all 21 members.
blocks.solution:
Find the two totals. The North total is 8 times 7. The South total is 13 times 13.

Together there are 225 visits and 21 people. Divide visits by people.

\(\frac{75}{7}\)

retry.feedback: The clubs have different sizes. Add all visits and divide by all the people.

blocks.html: An ordinary mean of the two group means gives equal weight to the groups. Check whether their sizes match before doing that.

blocks.title: Recover a missing group mean
blocks.prompt: Six pupils in one group average 2 trips to the library. There are 10 pupils in the other group. Together the 16 pupils average 7 trips. What is the mean for the group of 10?

field.label: Mean trips for the group of 10

blocks.hint: Recover the combined number of trips and the first group’s number of trips separately.
blocks.solution: The total is \(16\times7=112\). The first group accounts for \(6\times2=12\), leaving 100 trips for 10 pupils. Their mean is 10.

retry.feedback: 12 is the total for the smaller group. Take it away from the combined total, then divide by 10.

blocks.prompt:
The table gives the numbers of library visits made by the members of two clubs.

ClubMembersMean visits
North97
South1413

Find the mean number of visits per person for both clubs combined. Give an exact answer.
blocks.hint: North and South have different numbers of members. Multiply each group’s mean by its own headcount before combining.
blocks.solution:
Find the two totals. The North total is 9 times 7. The South total is 14 times 13.

Together there are 245 visits and 23 people. Divide visits by people.

\(\frac{245}{23}\)

retry.feedback: The clubs have different sizes. Add all visits and divide by all the people.

blocks.html: Show the combined numerator and denominator before dividing.

sections.title: Which outcomes belong to the event?
sections.label: Test both orders
sections.intro: Decide whether the event names one route or several routes. If the event is ‘at least one’, its complement often gives a single route. Draw or list enough outcomes to see which calculation is shorter.

blocks.html: For one route, multiply its consecutive probabilities. Add the probabilities of separate routes that can each give the event.

figure.alt: The two possible colours on each of two draws give BB, BW, WB and WW.
figure.caption: BW and WB have different orders. Add their probabilities to count one of each colour.

blocks.prompt:
A bag holds 3 blue counters and 8 white counters. Two counters are drawn one after the other. The first counter is kept out of the bag.

Find the probability of getting one counter of each colour, in either order.
blocks.hint: Start by writing blue then white and white then blue. The second denominator is 10 after the first counter is kept out.
blocks.solution:
List the orders BW and WB. The first draw is from 11 counters. The second draw is from 10 counters.

Each order has probability \(\frac{12}{55}\). Add the two probabilities.

\(\frac{24}{55}\)

retry.feedback: Your calculation gives one order. Include both BW and WB.

blocks.html: Writing down only blue then white misses white then blue. Writing the same fractions for both stages misses the removal.

blocks.title: Use the complement of at least one white
blocks.prompt: A bag contains four blue and four white counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of getting at least one white?
blocks.hint: The event fails only if both counters are blue. Find that one path first.
blocks.solution: Two blues have probability \(\frac48\times\frac37=\frac3{14}\). At least one white has probability \(1-\frac3{14}=\frac{11}{14}\).

retry.feedback: This is the probability of two blues. Subtract it from 1 to get the probability of at least one white.

blocks.prompt:
A bag holds 4 blue counters and 8 white counters. Two counters are drawn one after the other. The first counter is kept out of the bag.

Find the probability of getting one counter of each colour, in either order.
blocks.hint: Write both possible orders. Each starts with a different colour, but both second draws use the updated total.
blocks.solution:
List the orders BW and WB. The first draw is from 12 counters. The second draw is from 11 counters.

Each order has probability \(\frac{8}{33}\). Add the two probabilities.

\(\frac{16}{33}\)

retry.feedback: Your calculation gives one order. Include both BW and WB.

blocks.html: Label your order. After the first draw, check the new total before setting the second denominator.

sections.title: Which measurements scale twice?
sections.label: Choose a factor
sections.intro: A length factor acts on each side separately. When the problem gives only areas, divide the new area by the old area and take the positive square root to recover the length factor.

blocks.html: Perimeter uses the length scale factor. For area, each of the two dimensions contributes one factor, so the multiplier is its square.

figure.alt: A rectangle is doubled in both directions and contains four copies of the original area.
figure.caption: Doubling both lengths gives four original areas.

blocks.prompt:
A rectangular design is 12 cm by 18 cm. A larger copy is made with length scale factor \(4\).

Find the area of the larger design in square centimetres.
blocks.hint: The two old sides make 216 square centimetres. Each side grows by the same factor, so the area uses that factor twice.
blocks.solution:
Both side lengths are multiplied by \(4\). The area is multiplied by \(16\).

The old area is 216 square centimetres. Multiply it by the area factor.

\(3456\) square centimetres

retry.feedback: The factor is applied to both dimensions. Multiply the original area by the square of the factor.

blocks.html: Multiplying the area by the length factor stretches only one dimension. An enlargement changes both dimensions.

blocks.title: Find a corresponding length from two areas
blocks.prompt: A rectangular badge has area 24 square centimetres. A similar badge has area 54 square centimetres. An 8 cm side of the smaller badge corresponds to which length on the larger badge?
blocks.hint: Divide the areas to find the area factor, then recover the length factor before scaling the side.
blocks.solution: The area factor is \(\frac{54}{24}=\frac94\). The length factor is \(\frac32\), so the corresponding side is \(8\times\frac32=12\) cm.

retry.feedback: 18 cm applies the area factor to a length. Use the positive square root of the area factor for a length.

blocks.prompt:
A rectangular design is 3 cm by 10 cm. A larger copy is made with length scale factor \(4\).

Find the area of the larger design in square centimetres.
blocks.hint: You can find the new lengths separately before multiplying, or multiply the old area by the square of 4.
blocks.solution:
Both side lengths are multiplied by \(4\). The area is multiplied by \(16\).

The old area is 30 square centimetres. Multiply it by the area factor.

\(480\) square centimetres

retry.feedback: The factor is applied to both dimensions. Multiply the original area by the square of the factor.

blocks.html: Name the quantity before choosing its multiplier. State length or area units with the answer.

examples.title: Combining two groups fairly
examples.question:
The table gives the numbers of library visits made by the members of two clubs.

ClubMembersMean visits
North83
South1113

  1. Find the mean number of visits per person for both clubs combined. Give an exact answer.

    [2]

  2. Find the total number of visits by members of the larger club.

    [2]

  3. One member changes clubs but keeps the same number of visits. Explain what happens to the combined mean.

    [2]
solution: (a) Find the two totals. The North total is 8 times 3. The South total is 11 times 13.
Together there are 167 visits and 19 people. Divide visits by people.
(b) Each member contributes 13 visits on average. Multiply by 11 members.
(c) The move changes the groups. The inputs to the combined mean stay fixed.
It stays the same. The total number of visits and the total number of people are unchanged.

examples.title: Find a missing group mean
examples.question: A survey includes 5 senior volunteers and 15 junior volunteers. The 20 volunteers average 7 library visits each. The seniors average 4 visits. Find the junior volunteers’ mean.
solution: The whole survey accounts for \(20\times7=140\) visits. The seniors contribute \(5\times4=20\) visits.
The 15 juniors contribute \(140-20=120\) visits.
Divide by the junior headcount to get \(120\div15=8\) visits per junior on average.

examples.title: Two draws without replacement
examples.question:
A bag holds 4 blue counters and 5 white counters. Two counters are drawn one after the other. The first counter is kept out of the bag.

  1. Find the probability of getting one counter of each colour, in either order.

    [2]

  2. Find the probability of two blue counters.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the probability of blue usually changes between the first and second draws.

    [2]
solution: (a) List the orders BW and WB. The first draw is from 9 counters. The second draw is from 8 counters.
Each order has probability \(\frac{5}{18}\). Add the two probabilities.
(b) After drawing one blue counter, there are 3 blue counters left out of 8.
(c) The first draw determines which counts are used in the fraction for the second draw.
One counter has been removed. If it was blue, both the number of blue counters and the total fall. If it was white, only the total falls.

examples.title: Use the complement for at least one blue counter
examples.question: A bag contains 5 blue and 3 white counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that at least one counter is blue.
solution: The event fails only if both counters are white. That is one route, so use its probability first.
For two whites the branch probabilities are \(\frac38\) and \(\frac27\). Their product is \(\frac{3}{28}\).
The probability of at least one blue is \(1-\frac{3}{28}=\frac{25}{28}\). This includes two blues.

examples.title: A larger copy of a display
examples.question:
A rectangular design is 12 cm by 16 cm. A larger copy is made with length scale factor \(3\).

  1. Find the area of the larger design in square centimetres.

    [2]

  2. Find the perimeter of the larger design in centimetres.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the same multiplier cannot be used for both perimeter and area.

    [2]
solution: (a) Both side lengths are multiplied by \(3\). The area is multiplied by \(9\).
The old area is 192 square centimetres. Multiply it by the area factor.
\(1728\) square centimetres
(b) The perimeter is a length. Multiply the original perimeter 56 cm by \(3\) once.
(c) Writing each calculation using the two side lengths shows how often the scale factor appears.
The perimeter adds scaled lengths. The area multiplies two scaled lengths, so the factor occurs twice.

examples.title: Recover a length scale factor from two areas
examples.question: A rectangular poster has area 40 square centimetres. A similar poster has area 90 square centimetres. A 10 cm side of the smaller poster corresponds to a side of the larger poster. Find the larger side.
solution: The area factor is \(\frac{90}{40}=\frac94\). It is the square of the length scale factor.
The positive length scale factor is \(\sqrt{\frac94}=\frac32\).
The corresponding length is \(10\times\frac32=15\) cm.

glossary.definition: Total for all entries divided by the total number of entries.
A possible result, with order when it matters.
The multiplier that maps a length to its corresponding length.

revision.body:
Recover totals

Multiply each group mean by its headcount. Divide the combined total by the combined headcount.

Use a complement

For ‘at least one’, consider the outcome with none. Without replacement, update the counts before the second draw.

Recover a length factor

Divide the new area by the old area. Take the positive square root of that ratio to find the length factor.
